newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Storm over German gold plan prompts EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Storm over German gold plan prompts EMU jitters.

text.p: Europe's single currency plans looked increasingly shaky on Thursday as Germany's finance minister tried to reassure markets that a row with his powerful central bank would not derail the euro.

Theo Waigel rejected calls for his resignation after a stormy reaction to the power struggle between the government and the Bundesbank over controversial plans to revalue gold assets and boost Germany's flagging public finances.

Insisting the plan would go ahead and the euro would start on time in 1999, he told a hastily convened news conference in his home state of Bavaria: "Germany can meet EMU criteria even without the reserve revaluation."
The dollar jumped against the mark in European markets which buzzed with chatter of possible high-level resignations.
The scent of a left-wing victory in French elections on Sunday added to the EMU nervousness triggered by Wednesday's clash between Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his fiercely independent Bundesbank.
"It's a mess," one German economist said.
"It is getting to the stage were you can't even make an educated guess about what the next stage is," said Francis Breedon, senior foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.
In excited currency markets, the dollar climbed nearly two pfennigs to 1.7067 marks, boosted by its safe-haven reputation, but later eased back a touch 1.7002 in late European trade.
Desperate to start EMU on time, Kohl has warned that he will change the law to force the Bundesbank to pay into government coffers up to 20 billion marks ($11 billion) from the revalued gold.

Suspicions that Germany is cooking the books in a desperate bid to trim its deficits to make the grade for EMU have not only angered the proud central bank and German public opinion but also EU partners which Bonn argues are too weak to join EMU.
Any sign of falling back on creative accounting is seen as an invitation to less worthy economies such as Italy to join the single currency in its infancy.
Market expectations are that if the French left wins Sunday's election run-off, it will push for Italy and Spain to be among EMU's founding members -- watering down the euro.
Rome, criticised by Germany for its poor showing on fiscal rectitude, was quick to wade in, with treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi saying his country was no longer Europe's "ugly duckling".

Economists said the German row and French hesitancy meant EMU would now either be delayed or would go ahead, but in a broader and weaker format, posing serious credibility fears for what is designed to be one of the world's strongest currencies.
"The view (is) that this doesn't affect EMU going ahead on time in 1999 but the chances of broader EMU membership are more likely," said HSBC's Robert Prior.
Meanwhile, the European Commission, the single currency's watchdog, insisted all was well, maintaining that EMU would start on time in those countries meeting the qualifications.
"For me, there is no risk concerning EMU. I'm confident the German government will be ready in due time," Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy told reporters.
But he stressed that budget accounting principles must be respected and there would be no "fudging of the figures".
Bonn's high-risk strategy prompted widespread talk of political reputations being put at stake.

"(German Finance Minister Theo) Waigel now looks like he has no principles, resorting to the same sort of creative accounting tricks that he had accused other nations, like Italy and France, of using," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
German commentators said Kohl's gamble to ride roughshod over the Bundesbank and plough on with EMU could be his biggest in 14 years in office.
"He may have lost the 1998 election right there," remarked one Bonn insider, who asked not to be named.
Responding to market gossip, Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher "completely ruled out" the possibility that bank president Hans Tietmeyer planned to resign.
Waigel, on the brink of becoming Germany's longest-serving finance minister, said he was "very relaxed" and would remain in office.
